title: Chhath Puja Facts
usage: Randomly display one fact at a time on a website.

status_legend.verified: Supported by official/credible sources or widely documented practice.
status_legend.traditional: Religious/cultural belief or tradition; not necessarily independently historically verified.
status_legend.observed: Contemporary cultural observation; may vary by place.
status_legend.interpretive: Reasonable cultural interpretation rather than a hard historical fact.

facts.fact: Chhath Puja is a major Hindu festival dedicated to Surya, the Sun deity.
Chhath is especially prominent in Bihar and eastern Uttar Pradesh.
Chhath is also widely observed in Jharkhand and parts of Nepal.
Chhath Puja is also known as Surya Shashti.
The main Kartik Chhath observance occurs in the Hindu month of Kartik.
The festival is traditionally observed over four main days.
The four main stages are Nahay Khay, Kharna/Lohanda, Sandhya Arghya and Usha Arghya.
Nahay Khay is the first day of Chhath.
Nahay Khay emphasizes bathing, cleanliness and ritual preparation.
Homes are traditionally cleaned as part of Nahay Khay preparations.
The second day is called Kharna, also known as Lohanda in some traditions.
Kharna involves a day-long fast followed by an evening ritual meal.
Kheer made with rice and jaggery is a traditional Kharna preparation.
Fruits are commonly included in Kharna offerings.
The third day culminates in Sandhya Arghya to the setting Sun.
The fourth day culminates in Usha Arghya to the rising Sun.
One distinctive feature of Chhath is worship of both the setting and rising Sun.
Arghya is a ritual offering made to the Sun during Chhath.
Devotees commonly make Arghya while standing in water.
Rivers, ponds, lakes and other water bodies can serve as Chhath worship sites.
A Chhath ghat is a place where devotees gather near a water body for the rituals.
The person observing the main Chhath fast is commonly called a Vrati.
Both women and men can observe the Chhath vrat.
Chhath is known for strict fasting and self-discipline.
Some devotees observe a waterless fast during the strict fasting period.
The fast is completed after the concluding Usha Arghya.
Thekua is one of the best-known Chhath prasad items.
Thekua is traditionally made primarily from wheat flour and jaggery or sugar.
Thekua is often shaped with decorative moulds.
Seasonal fruits are important offerings during Chhath.
Sugarcane is a common Chhath offering and decoration.
Coconut is commonly included among Chhath offerings.
Bamboo baskets are strongly associated with Chhath offerings.
A daura is a traditional bamboo basket used to carry Chhath offerings.
A supa is a traditional bamboo winnowing basket used in Chhath rituals.
Kosi is a colorful ritual associated with the night of the third day in many traditions.
Kosi can involve a canopy made from sugarcane stalks.
Earthen lamps are commonly used in Kosi and Chhath decorations.
Chhath folk songs are an important part of the festival's cultural expression.
Bhojpuri is one of the major languages of traditional Chhath songs.
Maithili is another important language of Chhath folk songs.
Magahi also has a strong Chhath song tradition.
Chhath songs often address Surya Dev and Chhathi Maiya.
Chhath music often expresses family devotion and wishes for well-being.
Sharda Sinha became one of the most recognizable voices associated with Chhath music.
Sharda Sinha helped bring Bihari folk music to a much wider audience.
Chhathi Maiya is a popular maternal deity associated with Chhath.
Chhathi Maiya is commonly associated with Shashthi.
Shashthi is traditionally associated with protection of children and childbirth.
Chhath combines solar worship with traditions surrounding family and children's well-being.
Chhath has ancient roots in Indian traditions of Sun worship.
Government tourism sources describe Chhath as rooted in ancient Vedic traditions.
The existence of ancient Sun worship does not by itself prove that the modern four-day Chhath had exactly the same form in antiquity.
Traditional stories connect Chhath with figures from the Ramayana and Mahabharata.
Karna is associated with Surya in the Mahabharata tradition.
Popular Chhath traditions sometimes connect Karna's devotion to Surya with the festival.
Some Chhath traditions associate Draupadi and the Pandavas with Surya worship.
Popular traditions also connect Rama and Sita with Sun worship after their return to Ayodhya.
These epic origin stories are best presented as religious traditions or legends rather than independently proven history.
Deo Surya Mandir in Aurangabad district, Bihar, is an important Sun temple associated with Chhath.
Deo Surya Mandir is dedicated to Surya.
The area around Deo is an important pilgrimage center during Chhath.
Deo is traditionally associated by local accounts with the origin of Chhath, but this should be treated as a traditional claim rather than settled historical fact.
Bihar has several historically important Sun temples.
Kandaha Sun Temple in Saharsa district is associated with Surya worship.
Chhath is deeply connected with Bihari cultural identity.
Chhath is also important to Bhojpuri, Maithili and Magahi-speaking communities.
Chhath often brings migrant families back to their home regions.
Seasonal travel demand rises sharply around Chhath.
Special trains are often operated around the Chhath travel period.
Delhi has developed large public Chhath celebrations outside Bihar.
Mumbai hosts significant Chhath celebrations.
Kolkata has substantial Chhath observances.
Bengaluru and other Indian cities also host Chhath celebrations.
Temporary ghats allow Chhath to be observed in cities without traditional riverfronts.
Artificial ponds can be prepared for urban Chhath celebrations.
Municipal authorities often clean and prepare ghats before Chhath.
Large Chhath gatherings require traffic and crowd management.
Medical and emergency arrangements may be deployed at major Chhath sites.
Chhath has a major public and community dimension in addition to household worship.
Prasad is traditionally shared with relatives, neighbors and other community members.
Family members who are not fasting can still participate in Chhath preparations.
Children often participate by helping carry offerings or accompanying families to the ghat.
Bamboo craft workers can experience seasonal demand for Chhath baskets.
Fruit sellers commonly see increased demand during Chhath.
Sugarcane sellers commonly see increased demand during Chhath.
Chhath has strong associations with seasonal agricultural produce.
Rice is an important ingredient in several Chhath preparations.
Wheat flour is used for Thekua.
Jaggery is used in several traditional Chhath preparations.
The festival's offerings prominently feature natural and seasonal foods.
Chhath has a strong symbolic relationship with Sun, water, agriculture and life.
Cleanliness is a central value in Chhath preparation and observance.
Ritual food is often prepared with separate utensils and strict cleanliness practices.
Many Chhath households avoid onion and garlic in festival food.
Exact food and ritual rules can vary by family and region.
Chhath is not exclusively a women's festival even though women are prominent among Vratis.
Men can also observe the Chhath vrat.
Chhath is celebrated in Nepal's Terai and Madhesh regions.
Janakpur is an important Chhath celebration center in Nepal.
Chhath is observed around water bodies in Nepal as well as India.
Chhath traditions cross the India-Nepal cultural border.
Chhath has spread through migration to Indian metropolitan areas.
Chhath is also practiced by diaspora communities outside India and Nepal.
Diaspora communities may use artificial ponds when natural water bodies are unavailable.
Chaiti Chhath is another annual Chhath observance held in the month of Chaitra.
Kartik Chhath is generally the larger and more widely recognized Chhath observance.
Chaiti Chhath also follows the characteristic multi-day ritual structure.
Chhath is often called Chhath Mahaparv, emphasizing its cultural importance.
The word Chhath is associated with the sixth lunar day, Shashthi.
Chhath is unusual among major festivals because sunset is itself a major worship moment.
The festival's central worship can take place outdoors rather than inside a temple.
The horizon and natural light become part of the ritual setting during Arghya.
Water reflects sunlight during Arghya, creating a distinctive visual aspect of Chhath.
Chhath folk traditions have been transmitted orally across generations.
Modern recordings have helped Chhath songs reach audiences beyond their traditional regions.
YouTube and streaming services have expanded access to Chhath music.
Social media is now used to share Chhath greetings and coordinate community activities.
Online platforms allow people living far from home to participate remotely in Chhath culture.
Chhath demonstrates how an old ritual tradition can adapt to modern urban and digital life.
Traditional bamboo baskets remain an important visual symbol of Chhath.
Earthen diyas are commonly used to illuminate Chhath spaces.
Folk songs can be heard at Chhath ghats during evening worship.
Chhath gatherings can turn ordinary public spaces into temporary sacred spaces.
The festival combines personal austerity with large-scale community participation.
Chhath is often associated with prayers for family health, prosperity and well-being.
Devotees may undertake the vrat as an expression of gratitude as well as prayer.
The Sun is traditionally regarded as a source of light, energy and life.
Chhath's focus on water bodies makes river and pond cleanliness especially important to devotees.
Modern celebrations can create environmental challenges through plastic and crowd-generated waste.
Pollution of rivers can affect the experience and safety of Chhath gatherings.
Traditional Chhath materials include bamboo, earthen lamps and natural food offerings.
Chhath is often described as nature-oriented because Sun and water are central to its worship.
Chhath songs often express longing for home and family among migrant communities.
The festival can strengthen intergenerational transmission of recipes, songs and ritual knowledge.
Chhath can involve extensive volunteer and community coordination at public ghats.
Local governments can become deeply involved in preparing public Chhath infrastructure.
Chhath has become an important cultural event in many Indian cities with Purvanchali and Bihari communities.
The festival's regional variations mean there is no single universal Chhath procedure followed identically everywhere.
A good way to understand Chhath is as a living tradition combining devotion, family, nature, food, music and community.
